articles.summary: This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. One fall afternoon in Liberty, Mississippi, in 1961, a white Democratic former congressman and state legislator named E. H. Hurst shot Herbert Lee in the head. Hurst was angry that Lee, who was Black, had been trying to register other Black Mississippians to vote. An all-white jury accepted Hurst’s claim that he had acted in self-defense because Lee came at him with a tire iron. Donald Trump, now the sitting president of the United States, was 15 years old. This was how “negro law” worked in Jim Crow Mississippi, which was essentially a police state. Although many laws were race-neutral in their language, “in a society in which race mattered above all else, ‘negro law’ determined who was punished for what,” the historian Neil McMillen wrote in Dark Journey , his 1989 history of Mississippi. In the 1940s, the NAACP was “virtually forced to operate underground,” because in 1920, the state legislature had made it illegal to “possess or distribute” material that would “disturb relations between the races.” As late as 1961, a white man could shoot a Black man in broad daylight and get away with it.

There is no doubt that a lot of bad, big-government policies are in store. But if the prospect of Democrats returning to power is so terrifying, why on earth did Republicans elect a president and vice president as controversial as Donald Trump and J.D. Vance? Why did they support so many policies in clear opposition to the promotion of a free and virtuous society? Did they think a majority of voters would enjoy the result? You cannot spend years governing this way, adopting tariffs and other policies that raise the cost of living, defying a clear directive to lower prices from voters in the previous election, and then expect the fear of what Democrats might do to spare your party from accountability. stories.summary: US President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico if it doesn’t stop a migrant caravan heading for the border, ratcheting up tensions with the US’ biggest trading partner. Illegal crossings of the US-Mexico border have plummeted during Trump’s second term partly because Mexico, which sends the vast majority of its exports to its northern neighbor, has deployed troops to stem the flow and win over the White House. The Democratic Party’s recent electoral victories have lifted hopes of a warmer US welcome among would-be migrants. However, Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller — the architect of Washington’s draconian approach to immigration, including divisive raids — to become the president’s chief of staff has dashed hopes of a friendlier policy any time soon. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

articles.title: Why House Democrats might not have to cooperate with Jim Jordan
articles.author: Nicholas Wu
articles.summary: House Democrats are looking askance at Rep. Jim Jordan’s election as minority leader, given the Ohio Republican has few relationships across the aisle — but next year, they might not have to work with him much. Democrats are likely to put up bills at the beginning of next Congress that could draw some bipartisan support like a stock trading ban, but their cushy House majority is likely to eliminate the need for Republican support on key funding and rule votes. And the narrower House Republican minority will reduce the effectiveness of discharge petitions, which Democrats and a small bloc of Republicans used successfully this Congress to force votes. Republicans’ procedural hijinks on a veterans benefits bill this week won’t help cross-party ties: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark registered her objections with Republicans but was rebuffed about reversing course, though that courtesy has typically been extended to the House minority, according to a person familiar with the situation. — Nicholas Wu
